topic_tag: rectangle completed in the coordinate plane
subskill: perpendicular slope to locate a rectangle vertex
prompt: In the standard (x,y) coordinate plane, rectangle ABCD has vertices A(−6, 6) and B(5, 3), and vertex C lies on the x-axis. To the nearest hundredth of a coordinate unit, what is the length of diagonal AC ?
explanation: Side BC is perpendicular to side AB at B. The slope of AB is (3 − 6)/(5 − (−6)) = −3/11, so BC has slope 11/3. On y − 3 = (11/3)(x − 5), y = 0 gives x = 5 − 9/11 = 46/11, so C = (46/11, 0). Then AC = √((46/11 + 6)² + 6²) = √((112/11)² + 36) = 130/11 ≈ 11.82. The option "13.25" uses the reciprocal slope without changing its sign (−11/3), which puts C at (64/11, 0). The option "12.53" assumes side BC is vertical and takes C = (5, 0). The option "12.99" puts the right angle in the wrong place: it drops the perpendicular through A to the x-axis (as if D were the vertex on the axis) and completes the rectangle from there.
quantity_asked: the length of diagonal AC of the rectangle, 130/11 ≈ 11.82, after locating C on the x-axis from the perpendicular slope at B.

distractor_kind.13.25: perpendicular slope sign slip: −11/3 instead of 11/3. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: not an intermediate. (c) cheapest bounds: AC > AB = √130 ≈ 11.40 and AC ≥ √(130 + 3²) ≈ 11.79 (BC is at least B's height 3); 13.25 strictly above both. (d) real: reciprocal taken, sign not changed.
distractor_kind.12.53: BC assumed vertical, C = (5, 0). (a) no. (b) neighbouring: the point of the x-axis nearest B; not a bound on AC. (c) strictly above 11.79. (d) real: treats the rectangle as axis-aligned on that side.
distractor_kind.12.99: right angle at the wrong vertex: perpendicular through A meets the x-axis, rectangle completed from there. (a) no. (b) none. (c) strictly above 11.79. (d) real: vertex-label slip (the vertex on the axis taken as D).

bounds: v > AB = √130 ≈ 11.40 (diagonal longer than a side)
v ≥ √(130 + 9) ≈ 11.79 (BC at least the height of B above the axis)
mechanism: diagonal length by the distance formula
arith_class_check: Key 130/11 shows as a two-decimal value like every option; no integrality is implied (C's x-coordinate is 46/11).
one_sided_check: Key smallest. Three different errors (slope sign, vertical-side assumption, wrong vertex). The natural negate-only slip (slope 3/11) puts C at (−6, 0) and gives AC = 6, far BELOW the key; a student cannot read from the stem that slope slips raise AC.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 12.53 and 12.99, both two-decimal with a nonzero final digit; neither nicer.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest one-sided bounds: AC > AB ≈ 11.40 and, one step finer, AC ≥ √(AB² + 3²) ≈ 11.79 since BC is at least B's height above the axis. Both sit BELOW the key; all three distractors lie above them, on the key's side. No cheap upper bound separates 11.82 from 12.53 (6% apart).

self_audit.note: Smallest key; slope slips go both ways (negate-only gives 6); the only cheap bounds sit below the key. Perpendicular-bisector-to-x-axis items are live but differ (midpoint, intercept asked).

topic_tag: similar triangles cut by a parallel segment
prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = 10 centimeters, AC = 13 centimeters, and BC = 5 centimeters. Point D lies on side AB and point E lies on side AC so that segment DE is parallel to side BC. The perimeter of triangle ADE is equal to the perimeter of quadrilateral DBCE. To the nearest hundredth of a centimeter, what is the length of AE ?
explanation: Because DE ∥ BC, triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC; let k = AE/AC = AD/AB = DE/BC. The perimeter of ADE is 10k + 13k + 5k = 28k. The perimeter of DBCE is DB + BC + CE + ED = 10(1 − k) + 5 + 13(1 − k) + 5k = 28 − 18k. Setting 28k = 28 − 18k gives k = 28/46 = 14/23, so AE = 13(14/23) = 182/23 ≈ 7.91. The option "7.14" leaves side DE out of the quadrilateral's perimeter (28k = 28 − 23k, k = 28/51). The option "8.88" leaves DE out of the triangle's perimeter instead (23k = 28 − 18k, k = 28/41). The option "9.19" splits the AREA in half rather than the perimeter (k = 1/√2).
quantity_asked: the length AE when the parallel segment DE makes the two pieces' perimeters equal: 13·(14/23) ≈ 7.91.

distractor_kind.7.14: shared side DE omitted from the quadrilateral's perimeter. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: not an intermediate. (c) cheapest bounds: AE > AC/2 = 6.5 (at the midpoints the quadrilateral's perimeter is larger by BC/2, so k > 1/2) and AE < AC = 13; 7.14 strictly inside. (d) real: forgets the shared side belongs to both pieces.
distractor_kind.8.88: shared side DE omitted from the triangle's perimeter. (a) no. (b) none. (c) inside (6.5, 13). (d) real: the mirror-image omission.
distractor_kind.9.19: area condition used instead of perimeter (k = 1/√2). (a) no. (b) neighbouring setup: the equal-area cut; strictly inside (6.5, 13). (c) inside. (d) real: the familiar 'halve the triangle' scale factor.

bounds: v > AC/2 = 6.5 (k > 1/2: at the midpoints the quadrilateral's perimeter is larger)
v < AC = 13
mechanism: segment parallel to a side of a triangle
equal perimeters of the two pieces
arith_class_check: Key 182/23 ≈ 7.91 is a two-decimal non-terminating value like every option; no integrality is implied.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 7.91 and 8.88, both two-decimal with one integer digit and nonzero last digit; neither nicer.

self_audit.note: Interior key; errors both ways (drop DE from one piece or the other). Equal-area cuts are live (v26 vertical line), equal-perimeter parallel cut not found.

subskill: base edge from lateral area and face angle
prompt: The roof of a gazebo has the shape of the four triangular faces of a right pyramid with a square base: the top point of the roof is directly above the center of the square. Each of the four triangular faces of the roof makes an angle of 32° with the horizontal, and the total area of the four faces is 76 square meters. To the nearest hundredth of a meter, what is the length of each side of the square base of the roof?
explanation: Let s be the side of the square. In the right triangle formed by the top point, the center of the base, and the midpoint of a base edge, the horizontal leg is s/2 and the angle at the midpoint is 32°, so the slant height of a face is (s/2)/cos 32°. The four faces have total area 4 · (1/2) · s · (s/2)/cos 32° = s²/cos 32°. So s² = 76 cos 32° ≈ 64.45 and s ≈ 8.03. The option "6.35" uses sin 32° in place of cos 32° for the slant height. The option "7.55" treats 32° as the angle a lateral edge (corner ridge) makes with the horizontal, so the horizontal leg is half the diagonal of the square. The option "5.91" also counts the square base, setting s²/cos 32° + s² equal to 72.
quantity_asked: the base edge s of the square pyramid with s²/cos 32° = 76, s = √(76 cos 32°) ≈ 8.03 m.

distractor_kind.6.35: trig slip in the slant height: (s/2)/sin 32°, so s = √(76 sin 32°). (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: the face at 58°; strictly inside. (c) cheapest bounds: lateral area exceeds base area so s < √76 ≈ 8.72; with 32° < 45°, slant < (s/2)√2 so s > √(76/√2) ≈ 7.33; 6.35 is below 7.33 but the √2 step needs the slant relation itself. (d) real: sine/cosine confusion for the adjacent leg.
distractor_kind.7.55: angle placed on the corner ridge instead of the face: horizontal leg s/√2, lateral edge (s/√2)/cos 32°, slant from the edge by Pythagoras. (a) no. (b) neighbouring setup: the pyramid whose edges rise at 32°; strictly inside. (c) inside (7.33, 8.72). (d) real: reads the face angle as the edge angle.
distractor_kind.5.91: counts the base too: s²/cos 32° + s² = 72. (a) no. (b) neighbouring setup: total surface area 76; strictly inside. (c) below 7.33 but above 0. (d) real: total surface for the four roof faces.

6.35.error_kind: sine for cosine in slant height

7.55.error_kind: face angle read as edge angle

bounds: v < √76 ≈ 8.72 (the faces are steeper than flat, so their area exceeds the base area s²)
mechanism: square pyramid lateral area from face angle
lateral area = base area / cos θ
arith_class_check: All four options are two-decimal square roots of non-square products (64.45, 40.27, 56.95, 34.88); none integer, none singled out.
one_sided_check: Key largest. Distractors come from three different steps (trig ratio, which element the angle is on, which faces are counted). Natural errors on the OTHER side: using tan 32° (height taken as slant) gives s = √(76/tan 32°) ≈ 11.03, and multiplying by cos 32° instead of dividing (s²·cos 32° = 76) gives ≈ 9.47; both over, neither an option.
interior_parity_check: Interior options by value: 6.35 and 7.55; both two-decimal, nonzero last digit; neither nicer.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest one-sided bound: lateral area > base area, so s < √76 ≈ 8.72 (above the key; kills nothing). One step finer: since 32° < 45°, s > √(76/√2) ≈ 7.33; distractor 7.55 lies on the key's side of it. The counter errors 9.47 and 11.03 lie above the key.

subskill: vector to a point dividing a side
prompt: In the standard (x,y) coordinate plane, ABCD is a parallelogram with vertices in that order. The vector from A to B is u = ⟨4, −5⟩, and the vector from A to D is v = ⟨2, 4⟩. Point P lies on side CD so that DP is twice as long as PC. To the nearest hundredth, what is the magnitude of the vector from A to P ?

So AP = ⟨2 + 8/3, 4 − 10/3⟩ = ⟨14/3, 2/3⟩, and |AP| = √(196 + 4)/3 = √200/3 ≈ 4.71. The option "4.07" reverses the ratio, v + (1/3)u. The option "5.82" travels along the wrong pair of sides, u + (2/3)v. The option "7.36" subtracts, v − (2/3)u, treating DC as pointing opposite to AB.

(c) cheapest bounds: ||v| − (2/3)|u|| ≈ 0.20 ≤ |AP| ≤ |v| + (2/3)|u| ≈ 8.74, also |AP| ≤ |v| + |u| ≈ 10.88; 4.07 strictly inside. (d) real: reads DP:PC backwards.

topic_tag: sector area from a chord and an inscribed angle
subskill: inscribed angle to central angle, then radius
prompt: Points A, B, and C lie on a circle with center O. Chord AC is 11 centimeters long. Point B lies on the major arc AC, and the measure of ∠ABC is 54°. To the nearest tenth of a square centimeter, what is the area of sector AOC, the region bounded by radii OA and OC and the minor arc AC ?
explanation: The inscribed angle ABC intercepts minor arc AC, so central angle AOC = 2(54°) = 108°. In isosceles triangle AOC, half the chord is opposite half the central angle: 5.5 = r sin 54°, so r = 5.5/sin 54° ≈ 6.798. The sector's area is (108/360)πr² ≈ 0.3(π)(46.22) ≈ 43.6 square centimeters. The option "69.2" treats 54° as the central angle (r = 5.5/sin 27°, sector of 54°). The option "31.5" uses the whole central angle in the half-chord relation, r = 5.5/sin 108°. The option "82.5" finds r from the law of cosines but drops the sign of cos 108°: 121 = 2r²(1 − 0.309) instead of 2r²(1 + 0.309).

(b) neighbouring setup: the sector a 54° central angle would give; strictly inside. (c) cheapest bound: r ≥ 5.5 (a chord is at most a diameter) gives area ≥ 0.3π(5.5²) ≈ 28.5; no cheap upper bound without r; 69.2 strictly above 28.5. (d) real: the most common inscribed-angle slip.

topic_tag: law of sines in a sloped-ground sighting
subskill: law of sines with angles read off a slope
prompt: A vertical radio mast stands on a hillside that rises at a constant angle of 14° above the horizontal. Point P is on the hillside, downhill from the base of the mast, and the distance from P up the slope to the base of the mast is 44 meters; P, the base, and the mast all lie in one vertical plane. From P, the angle of elevation of the top of the mast, measured from the horizontal, is 33°. To the nearest hundredth of a meter, what is the height of the mast?
explanation: Let B be the base and T the top of the mast. In triangle PBT, the angle at P is between the slope (14° above horizontal) and the line of sight (33° above horizontal), so ∠TPB = 33° − 14° = 19°. At B, the vertical mast and the downhill slope make ∠PBT = 90° + 14° = 104°. So ∠PTB = 180° − 19° − 104° = 57°. By the law of sines, BT/sin 19° = PB/sin 57°, so BT = 44 sin 19°/sin 57° ≈ 17.08 meters. (Check with right triangles: P is 44 cos 14° ≈ 42.69 m horizontally from the mast and 44 sin 14° ≈ 10.64 m below its base; the top is 42.69 tan 33° ≈ 27.73 m above P, and 27.73 − 10.64 ≈ 17.08.) The option "16.75" finds the base's rise as 44 tan 14° instead of 44 sin 14°. The option "14.76" pairs the 44-meter side with the 104° angle at the base instead of the 57° angle opposite it. The option "12.61" uses sin 33° instead of tan 33° for the sight line's rise.
quantity_asked: the height BT of the mast, 44 sin 19°/sin 57° ≈ 17.08 m

distractor_kind.16.75: rise of the base above P taken as 44·tan 14° (tangent for sine on the slope step). (a) no parameter extreme. (b) not an intermediate of the solution. (c) cheap bounds: BT < 44 tan 33° − 44 sin 14° ≈ 17.93 (P's horizontal distance is less than 44) and BT > 44 sin 19° ≈ 14.32 (sin 57° < 1): strictly inside. (d) real: the slope's rise computed as run·tan with the slope distance as the run.
distractor_kind.14.76: law of sines with the 44-m side paired with the 104° base angle (sin 104° = cos 14°) instead of the 57° angle opposite it. (a) no. (b) no. (c) inside (14.32, 17.93). (d) real: side-angle pairing slip.

(c) below the 14.32 bound, which needs the law of sines set up (not cheap); above every cheap bound (BT > 0; top above P: BT > 10.64). (d) real: trig-ratio slip.

12.61.error_kind: sine for tangent on sight line

v > 44 sin 19° ≈ 14.32 (from the law of sines, since sin 57° < 1; not cheap)

subskill: kite diagonal via law of cosines and area
prompt: The frame of a toy kite is quadrilateral ABCD, in which AB = AD = 50 centimeters, CB = CD = 80 centimeters, and the measure of ∠ABC is 110°. A straight wooden spar runs from vertex B to vertex D. To the nearest hundredth of a centimeter, what is the length of the spar BD ?
explanation: Diagonal AC splits the kite into congruent triangles ABC and ADC, and the other diagonal BD is perpendicular to AC and bisected by it. In triangle ABC, AC² = 50² + 80² − 2(50)(80) cos 110° ≈ 8,900 + 2,736.2 = 11,636.2, so AC ≈ 107.87. The area of triangle ABC is (1/2)(50)(80) sin 110° ≈ 1,879.4, and it also equals (1/2)(AC)(h), where h is the distance from B to AC, so h ≈ 2(1,879.4)/107.87 ≈ 34.85. Since BD = 2h, BD ≈ 69.69 cm. Placing the 110° angle at A, between the two 50-cm sides, gives 2(50) sin 55° ≈ 81.92; taking the area of triangle ABC as (1/2)(50)(80) without sin 110° gives 74.16; using + instead of − in the law of cosines (AC ≈ 78.51) gives 95.75.

distractor_kind.81.92: puts the 110° angle at the top vertex A, between the two equal 50-cm sides, so BD = 2·50·sin 55°. (a) no parameter extreme. (b) neighbouring setup: kite with ∠BAD = 110°; strictly inside (0, 100). (c) cheapest bound: BD < AB + AD = 100; inside. (d) real: angle placed at the wrong vertex.
distractor_kind.95.75: sign slip in the law of cosines (+2ab cos C), so AC ≈ 78.51 and BD = 2·1,879.4/78.51. (a) no. (b) neighbouring setup: the kite with ∠ABC = 70°; strictly inside. (c) inside (0, 100). (d) real: cosine of an obtuse angle taken as positive.
distractor_kind.74.16: drops sin 110° from the area: takes the area of triangle ABC as (1/2)(50)(80) = 2,000, so h = 4,000/107.87 and BD ≈ 74.16. (a) no. (b) neighbouring setup: area of a right triangle with legs 50 and 80; strictly inside. (c) inside (0, 100). (d) real: (1/2)ab used without sin C.

v < 160 (BD < CB + CD)

topic_tag: area of a uniform border around a regular hexagon
subskill: apothem grows by the border width, not the side
prompt: A patio is shaped like a regular hexagon with sides 3.4 meters long. A walkway 1.7 meters wide surrounds the patio. The outer edge of the walkway is also a regular hexagon, and each of its six sides is parallel to a side of the patio and 1.7 meters from it. To the nearest hundredth of a square meter, what is the area of the walkway?
explanation: A regular hexagon with side s has apothem (s√3)/2 and area (3√3/2)s². The patio's apothem is 3.4(√3/2) ≈ 2.944 m. Moving every side out 1.7 m raises the apothem to ≈ 4.644 m, so the outer side is 4.644·(2/√3) ≈ 5.363 m (the side grows by 2(1.7)/√3, not by 1.7). Walkway area = (3√3/2)(5.363² − 3.4²) ≈ 44.69 square meters. Equivalently: six 3.4-by-1.7 rectangles (34.68) plus six corner pieces, each two right triangles with legs 1.7 and 1.7/√3 (total 6(1.7²)/√3 ≈ 10.01). The option "37.54" adds 1.7 to the side length.
